text: 2 With prior funding from DOE, the Long Island Biofuels Alliance laid the groundwork for harnessing the potential of duckweed as a bioenergy crop including a survey of fatty acid and TAG composition across 30 Lemnaceae species, a preliminary constraint-based model of carbon flux, a reliable and rapid protocol for stable transformation of Lemna japonica, and gene-knockdown by artificial miRNA. A patent (US9957514B2) was issued for these last two advances in 2018. Building on these accomplishments, support from this award enabled us to further expand critical genomic and epigenomic resources available for the study and engineering of duckweeds (Ernst et al. 2025), and to complete design-build-test-learn cycles that culminated in the successful engineering of high oil duckweeds. We shared our findings with the public and scientific community in a series of peer-reviewed publications highlighted below, data depositions in public repositories, and the lemna.org website. Critically, under the support of this award, we successfully reengineered metabolism in duckweeds, dramatically increasing oil content by diverting a substantial portion of accumulated carbon from starch (Liang et al. 2023). This sets the stage for the use of fast growing aquatic duckweeds as robust, highly productive sources of biodiesel, with the capacity to outperform soybean oil crops. The design principles and technologies we developed will have applications in other energy crops. Lemnaceae Genomics At the time this award was issued in 2017, the Martienssen lab had produced draft genome assemblies of Lemna gibba and Lemna japonica, but only one complete duckweed genome sequence had been published - that of Spirodela polyrhiza, the giant duckweed. Subsequently, the Lam lab and collaborators incorporated PacBio long-read sequencing, optical maps and DNA FISH to correct chromosome-level misassemblies in the initial reference, and establishing the second reference genome for S. polyrhiza (Hoang et al. 2018).
